## Section III: Comprehension (10 marks)

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions below it. It is important to read the questions and understand them.

**The sperm that never dies**

There are many advances in science almost every day and some of them have obvious pleasant consequences for mankind. However, it is not always easy to make up one's mind about the usefulness of other scientific work.

Imagine a mouse impregnating a cat or a bull impregnating a horse or, worse still, an elephant impregnating a deer. Can you imagine a man fathering a child, or one hundred children, a century after his death? This may sound preposterous or quite stupid, but a team of researchers at the University of Pennsylvania in the United States of America have reported that they have made scientific progress. They claim that they have frozen spermatogonial stem cells (these are the cells that make sperm), defrosted them, and brought them back to life. They have also claimed that they have taken stem cells from rats and implanted them in mice, which have then produced fully functional rat sperm.

The first experiment is, by itself, something of a reproductive achievement. Being able to keep the cells on ice is thus a lot more useful than the already common practice of freezing sperm itself: sperm lasts only so long, but a sperm factory can, in theory, go on forever. That could be comforting to men about to undergo, say, radiation treatment or chemotherapy, which can destroy stem cells and render patients permanently infertile. These men may avoid this problem by having their stem cells removed, frozen, and re-implanted after treatment.

Stem cells can give rise to new stem cells, which can then be harvested and frozen in turn. As a result, says Pennsylvania veterinary physiologist Ralph Brinster, a co-author of both studies, "we can make any individual male biologically immortal".

The second experiment is equally interesting. If rat stem cells can produce rat sperm while living in a mouse's testicles, then it is plausible that any mammalian species can play host to the stem cells of any other. This, for example, could help biologists to preserve the genetic material from endangered species. However, the possibility of abuse is always there. Imagine that some women may want to have sperm generated from the stem cells of one of their idols. Or that some racists or crazy politicians may want to dictate the type of stem cells to be imposed on people. The dangers are endless, and it is difficult to predict what the future holds in store if there is a free-for-all.

(Culled and adapted from *Time Magazine*, June 10, 1996)

**Questions**

1. What scientific innovation have researchers in Pennsylvania achieved? (1 mark)

2. How were sperms preserved before stem cells were used? (1 mark)

3. Explain what Ralph Brinster means by saying "we can make any individual male biologically immortal". (2 marks)

4. How can environmentalists benefit from this new advance in science? (2 marks)

5. Stem cells are more reliable for reproductive regeneration than sperms. True or false? Justify your opinion. (2 marks)

6. Do you think scientists should be allowed to carry out experiments which can lead to changes in the way the human body functions? Justify your opinion. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
To answer a comprehension question fully, never simply copy a sentence from the passage: identify the exact piece of information the question asks for, quote the relevant words from the text as evidence, and then reformulate that evidence in your own words to show that you have understood it, not merely located it. For a "true or false, justify" question, always state your choice clearly first, then support it with a specific reason drawn from the text. For a personal-opinion question, give a clear position and justify it with at least one concrete reason, even though more than one answer can be valid.

## 1. Scientific innovation achieved by the Pennsylvania researchers

The researchers "have frozen spermatogonial stem cells [...], defrosted them, and brought them back to life". In other words, they have succeeded in preserving the cells that produce sperm by freezing, and in reviving them afterwards so that they still function normally, which they also demonstrated a second time by implanting rat stem cells into mice, which then "produced fully functional rat sperm".

## 2. How sperm was preserved before stem cells were used

Before this discovery, the text explains that scientists relied on "the already common practice of freezing sperm itself". The passage adds that this older method has a limitation that the new one does not: "sperm lasts only so long", meaning that frozen sperm cells can only be preserved and remain usable for a limited period of time.

## 3. Meaning of "we can make any individual male biologically immortal"

Ralph Brinster does not mean that a man's body can physically live forever. He means that because "stem cells can give rise to new stem cells, which can then be harvested and frozen in turn", a man's capacity to reproduce can be preserved and renewed indefinitely, since the supply of stem cells never runs out the way frozen sperm eventually does. In this specific sense, a man's reproductive potential, his ability to father children, could in theory continue "forever", even long after his own death, which is what "biologically immortal" refers to here, not immortality of the body itself.

## 4. How environmentalists can benefit from this advance

The text states that "this... could help biologists to preserve the genetic material from endangered species", since "any mammalian species can play host to the stem cells of any other". Environmentalists could therefore use this technique to store and later reproduce the genetic material of animals threatened with extinction, by keeping their stem cells frozen and implanting them in a host species when needed, which would help prevent the definitive loss of endangered species' genetic material.

## 5. True or false: stem cells are more reliable than sperm for reproductive regeneration

**True.** The text explicitly contrasts the two methods: ordinary frozen sperm "lasts only so long", meaning its usable lifespan is limited, whereas "a sperm factory [built from stem cells] can, in theory, go on forever" because stem cells continually "give rise to new stem cells" that can be harvested and frozen again. This capacity for indefinite self-renewal makes stem cells a more durable and reliable source for reproductive regeneration than a finite, one-time supply of frozen sperm.

## 6. Personal opinion: should scientists be allowed to carry out experiments that change how the human body functions?

This is a personal-opinion question, and a well justified answer defending either position is acceptable. One reasonable position is a qualified "yes, but only within strict limits": such experiments can bring real benefits, for instance helping men made infertile by chemotherapy to have children again, as the passage describes, or helping preserve endangered species. However, the passage itself warns of "the possibility of abuse", such as the disturbing example of "some racists or crazy politicians" wanting "to dictate the type of stem cells to be imposed on people". Scientific research that alters human biological functions should therefore be permitted, but only under strict ethical supervision (informed consent, independent oversight committees, clear legal limits) that separates genuinely beneficial medical applications from uses that could harm human dignity or be turned into tools of discrimination.

### Piège à éviter
Do not answer a comprehension question with a sentence copied word for word from the passage: examiners specifically check for reformulation in your own words, in addition to accurate textual evidence, and a pure copy-paste answer is penalised even when it contains the "right" words.

### Conseil
For a "true or false, justify" question, always state your answer as the very first word of your response ("True." or "False.") before giving your justification: this makes your position unambiguous to the examiner even if the rest of your explanation is not perfectly worded.

incertitudes: Le texte source contenait plusieurs coquilles de saisie/scan visiblement fautives, corrigées dans l'énoncé reformulé sans en changer le sens : 'mmd' corrigé en 'mind', '1o' corrigé en 'a lot', 'a/deer' corrigé en 'a deer', et 'not got the death of' complété en 'not got over the death of'.

La question 6 est une question d'opinion personnelle : la position défendue dans le corrigé (autorisation encadrée par une supervision éthique stricte) est une réponse possible parmi d'autres positions également valables si elles sont correctement justifiées.
